Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk deployment via 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task launching Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk/LurkProxy deployment step where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs a staging batch script from the user's Videos or Desktop folder to install the loader service. Anchored on the exact task name, batch paths and the two published batch-script MD5s. Rationale: Uses the verbatim task name 'GoogleUpDate' from the article code block, the exact staging paths C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat and Desktop\auto.bat, and the two published batch MD5s (6ecf84... and b874123...) — all attacker-chosen, high-fidelity strings. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update/Chrome update scheduled tasks named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine' (note different casing/spacing — GoogleUpDate is the impostor)
  • Admin-authored batch scripts stored under a user's Videos or Desktop folder for ad-hoc automation
  • Software-deployment tooling that stages .bat files on Desktop before running
  • Pen-test/red-team tooling using schtasks for lateral execution
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents tree on the host — confirm the task ran as SYSTEM immediately after creation and whether it invoked sc.exe/1.bat to create a service (NgcCIntSvc/Cusrxsrv/etc.). 2) Contain: delete the GoogleUpDate task, isolate the host, and capture the referenced .bat and any DLL it drops for hashing against the loader IOCs. 3) Hunt: sweep for the loader service names and C2 domain dns.multitoconference.com across the estate; check which admin account created the task (remote creation implies stolen creds).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
    or MD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
    or InitiatingProcessMD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or CommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy loader service registration (ServiceMain=RegisterService loading oleasapi.dll/msbasesysdc.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts the loader install step where a service is created whose ServiceMain parameter is set to the export 'RegisterService' and whose ServiceDll is one of the named loader DLLs. Covers the custom loader execution/payload-decryption stage flagged by the reviewer. Rationale: Anchors on the article's distinctive loader mechanics: ServiceMain param pointing at the non-standard export 'RegisterService', the exact loader DLL names oleasapi.dll (MD5 082d49ef...) and msbasesysdc.dll, and the attacker-chosen service names. Legit service DLLs almost never store 'RegisterService' as ServiceMain. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Hyper-V integration services (vmicvss, vmictimesync) — note the impostor is vmictimerosync/vmicagent with altered spelling
  • Genuine PNRPHostSvc / peer-networking service reconfiguration (excluded from the name list for this reason)
  • Third-party service-DLL products that legitimately set a custom ServiceMain export name
  • Backup/EDR agents re-registering service DLLs during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmictimesync" or RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmicvss")
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host dump the service registry key and the referenced DLL; hash it against 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069 and check for the RegisterService/Refresh exports. 2) Contain: stop and delete the malicious service, isolate the host, and preserve the DLL and the C: volume serial (used as loader XOR key-2). 3) Hunt: pivot from the DLL to svchost network connections toward the LurkProxy/OctLurk C2 IPs and to any GoogleUpDate task; sweep other hosts for the same service names.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName in~ ("ServiceDll","ImagePath") and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
    or RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\NgcCIntSvc", @"\Services\Cusrxsrv", @"\Services\specitsrc", @"\Services\cmtastsvc", @"\Services\vmictimerosync", @"\Services\vmicagent")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
    or ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc","vmictimerosync","vmicagent")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to named backdoor infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host communication with the published OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses (many on dynamic-DNS providers, backdoor sockets on TCP/443). High-fidelity IOC match tying an endpoint to the campaign's command-and-control. Rationale: Direct match on the article's Indicators-of-Compromise section: 15 C2 domains (incl. dynamic-DNS gleeze.com/kozow.com/casacam.net/accesscam.org used by the backdoors) and 11 C2 IPs, including dns.multitoconference.com (OctLurk, TCP/443) and 154.196.162.76 (LurkProxy). Projecting InitiatingProcessFileName surfaces the svchost/service host that beacons. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/

OctLurk victim-fingerprinting recon command burst (chcp 1256 + qwinsta + klist + tasklist) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-compromise fingerprinting sequence OctLurk runs through its command shell plugin: switching the code page to 1256 (Arabic), enumerating sessions with qwinsta, listing Kerberos logon sessions with klist sessions, and running TASKLIST /V — several fired from one parent within minutes. Rationale: Built from the article's exact fingerprinting command table (chcp 1256, powershell $PSVersionTable, qwinsta, klist sessions, TASKLIST /V). chcp 1256 (Arabic code page, matching the Syrian/MoFA victimology) plus the burst of session/process discovery from a single parent within 10 minutes is far more specific than any single LOLBin. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1082 T1057 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin interactively troubleshooting RDP sessions (qwinsta) and Kerberos (klist) on a server
  • Logon scripts that call chcp for localization on Arabic-locale endpoints
  • Monitoring/inventory agents running tasklist /V periodically
  • PowerShell profiling scripts querying $PSVersionTable during onboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe","explorer.exe","taskmgr.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process of the command burst — a cmd.exe spawned by svchost/an unknown service DLL (not an interactive shell) strongly indicates the OctLurk command-shell plugin. 2) Contain: if parent is a suspicious service host, isolate and capture the DLL. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/timeframe with C2 beacons (UC3) and follow-on credential dumping (UC5) or FSCAN (UC6); check whether chcp 1256 aligns with Arabic-language victim targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "chcp.com" and ProcessCommandLine has "1256")
    or FileName =~ "qwinsta.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "klist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sessions")
    or (FileName =~ "tasklist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/V")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(FileName), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chcp.com" and CommandLine has "1256")
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\qwinsta.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\klist.exe" and CommandLine has "sessions")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" and CommandLine has "/V")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(NewProcessName), Cmds=make_set(CommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@CommandLine:*"chcp 1256"* OR @Image:(*\qwinsta.exe OR *\Qwinsta.exe) OR @CommandLine:*"klist sessions"* OR @CommandLine:*"TASKLIST /V"* OR @CommandLine:*PSVersionTable*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/chcp\s+1256|klist\s+sessions|tasklist\s+\/v|\$PSVersionTable/i OR ImageFileName=/\\qwinsta\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 3

Impacket secretsdump credential dumping in OctLurk post-compromise AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of Impacket's secretsdump used by the actor for credential dumping (SAM/LSA/NTDS) during lateral movement. Detects the secretsdump invocation and its DCSync-style '-just-dc' argument pattern regardless of interpreter or compiled packaging. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Impacket — secretsdump' in post-compromise credential harvesting. Anchoring on the module name and the DCSync-style '-just-dc ...@target' argument shape catches both python and compiled/renamed Impacket packaging without relying on a hash the report says was unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / authorized penetration tests running Impacket secretsdump
  • AD migration or password-audit tooling that legitimately performs DCSync
  • Security researchers testing Impacket in a lab within the same tenant
  • Backup solutions invoking ntds util (different arg shape — should not match '-just-dc @')
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-adaudit","svc-pwaudit")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the account context; confirm whether '-just-dc' (DCSync against a DC) or SAM/LSA local dump, and whether the target host is a domain controller. 2) Contain: isolate source host, force-reset any exposed krbtgt/privileged and service accounts, and revoke Kerberos tickets if DCSync succeeded. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 loader presence and UC3 C2 on the same host; look for FSCAN recon (UC6) that preceded the credential dump and unusual admin logons to the DC.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc" and ProcessCommandLine has "@")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc-ntlm" and ProcessCommandLine has "-hashes")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (CommandLine has "-just-dc" and CommandLine has "@")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FSCAN internal network reconnaissance fan-out AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the internal reconnaissance stage where the actor runs FSCAN to sweep the network — one source touching many internal hosts across scanner ports (SSH, SMB, RDP, MSSQL, MySQL, Redis) in a short window, plus direct fscan binary execution. Rationale: The article names 'Network scan: FSCAN' as post-compromise activity. Detection combines the direct fscan.exe process (Sigma) with the behavioral fan-out (one internal source hitting >=50 hosts on FSCAN's default scan ports within 5 min), which survives binary renaming. Sentinel query fixed to group on SourceIP/SourceHostName (valid CommonSecurityLog columns) instead of the non-existent DeviceName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS) sweeping the estate
  • Network/asset-discovery tools (Lansweeper, nmap-based inventory)
  • SCCM/endpoint-management client-push connectivity checks across a subnet
  • Backup or monitoring servers probing SMB/SQL on many hosts
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("scanner01","nessus01","lansweeper01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus-service.exe","nmap.exe","Nessus.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) and whether the source host is an approved scanner; an unknown/renamed binary spawned by a service host is high-signal for FSCAN. 2) Contain: isolate the source host and block its lateral SMB/RDP/SQL traffic. 3) Hunt: correlate with the loader (UC2), C2 (UC3) and any subsequent secretsdump (UC5); map which internal hosts responded on 445/3389 to scope likely lateral targets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| where RemotePort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(RemoteIP), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to /24 estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(DestinationIP), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort, 20), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, SourceHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc

Browser credential-store theft via OctLurk browser password decryptor AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OctLurk 'Browser Password Decryptor' capability: a non-browser process reading Chromium/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Local State' (AES key) or Firefox 'logins.json'/'key4.db' to steal stored passwords. Rationale: The article lists 'Browser Password Decryptor' / browser password stealer as an OctLurk capability. High-fidelity signal is a non-browser process touching the Chromium 'Login Data' + 'Local State' pair (Local State holds the DPAPI-wrapped AES key) or Firefox key4.db/logins.json — the exact files any browser-credential stealer must read. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as browser file-read telemetry isn't in their standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync agents (OneDrive, Google Drive, corporate backup) copying user profile directories
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic tools inventorying browser artifacts
  • Browser migration/import utilities reading another browser's profile
  • Antivirus on-access scans opening the SQLite stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","googledrivesync.exe","Dropbox.exe","MsMpEng.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process and its parent; a process from an unusual path or a service host reading both Login Data and Local State is a strong stealer indicator. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force password resets for accounts whose credentials are likely stored in that browser profile (prioritize privileged/SSO). 3) Hunt: correlate with OctLurk loader/C2 on the same host, look for archive utilities (WinRAR/7z) staging the harvested data, and check for outbound transfer to the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","Web Data","cookies.sqlite")
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","OneDrive.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\User Data\Local State", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
    or TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","Login Data","Local State")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-browser access to browser credential stores
id: 2f9b6a41-8c73-4e05-b1d8-6a0f3c7e2d94
description: Detects a non-browser process reading Chromium/Edge Login Data or Local State, or Firefox logins.json/key4.db - consistent with OctLurk's browser password decryptor.
references:
  - https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/05
tags:
  - attack.t1555.003
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: file_access
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\User Data\Default\Login Data'
      - '\User Data\Local State'
      - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
      - '\logins.json'
      - '\key4.db'
  filter_browsers:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\chrome.exe'
      - '\msedge.exe'
      - '\firefox.exe'
      - '\brave.exe'
      - '\opera.exe'
      - '\msedgewebview2.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_browsers
level: high
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo TargetFileName=/(\\User Data\\.*\\Login Data|\\User Data\\Local State|\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles\\.*(key4\.db|logins\.json))/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|opera|msedgewebview2)\.exe$/i
| table([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*\\Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\Local State" OR Filesystem.file_name=key4.db OR Filesystem.file_name=logins.json) AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN (chrome.exe,msedge.exe,firefox.exe,brave.exe,opera.exe,msedgewebview2.exe) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\*\\Login Data" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\User Data\\Local State" OR Filesystem.file_name=key4.db OR Filesystem.file_name=logins.json) AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN (chrome.exe,msedge.exe,firefox.exe,brave.exe,opera.exe,msedgewebview2.exe) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.file_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/

date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows

    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Service Persistence via sc.exe with User-Writable Path
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0e
status: experimental
description: |
    sc.exe create with the binary path under \Users\, \AppData\,
    \ProgramData\, or \Temp\ — service-install persistence outside
    legitimate program directories.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1543/003/
author: Clankerusecase

    - attack.t1543.003

            - '\Users\'
            - '\AppData\'
            - '\ProgramData\'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="sc.exe" AND Processes.process="*create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*\Users\*" OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*"
        OR Processes.process="*\ProgramData\*" OR Processes.process="*\Temp\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
        where Registry.registry_path="*\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*"
          AND Registry.registry_value_name="ImagePath"
          AND (Registry.registry_value_data="*\Users\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\AppData\*"
            OR Registry.registry_value_data="*\Temp\*")
        by Registry.dest, Registry.registry_path, Registry.registry_value_data, Registry.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`]
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer

status: experimental
description: |

    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.

    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/

      AND (Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\windows\temp\in.bat*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Users\Public\Pictures\AnyDesk.exe*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Users\Public\Libraries\msect\dev0*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\Users\Public\Libraries\msect\dev1*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*%LOCALAPPDATA%\Google\Chrome\User*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*%APPDATA%\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*C:\ProgramData\1.bat*" OR Filesystem.file_name IN ("oleasapi.dll","auto.bat","msbasesysdc.dll","in.bat","adobe.exe","secretsdump.py","anydesk.exe","64.exe","fc.exe","netsetsvc.exe","nvgwls.exe","rtksmbus.exe","rtkngui64.exe","nvml.dll","vulkan-1.dll"))
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.process_name,
       Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
]
| append [
  | tstats summariesonly=false count
      from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry
      where Registry.action IN ("created","modified")
        AND (Registry.registry_path="*HKLM\\SOFTWARE\\Microsoft\\Windows*")
      by Registry.dest, Registry.process_name, Registry.registry_path,
         Registry.registry_value_name, Registry.registry_value_data
  | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
]

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Installation. Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) · [LLM] Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains

Watering-hole exploit-script delivery from jshosting[.]me (AnySign4PC drive-by) AIDelivery High
Hunts endpoint contact with jshosting[.]me, the domain AhnLab/KISA attribute to distribution of the version-specific AnySign4PC exploit scripts in both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains. Because the exploit runs with no download prompt, the DNS/HTTP callout to this domain is often the earliest host-visible signal of the drive-by. Rationale: jshosting[.]me is a hard IOC confirmed by AhnLab as the exploit-script distribution domain shared by both the espionage and Gunra intrusions; a corporate host resolving it is high-fidelity given it is not a legitimate service. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1189 T1608.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or SOC analyst detonating the sample in a sandbox that egresses through the corporate resolver
  • Threat-intel enrichment/crawler tooling actively resolving IOC domains
  • DNS sinkhole/RPZ appliance logging the query as it blocks it (verify answer is sinkhole IP)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !has "sandbox"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcess making the callout — a browser process is consistent with the watering-hole drive-by; confirm the user visited a Korean news/healthcare/education site immediately prior. 2) Contain: block jshosting[.]me at proxy/DNS, isolate the host, and snapshot AnySign4PC version (flag 1.1.4.4–1.1.4.6). 3) Hunt: on the same host look for AnySign4PC.exe spawning children/writing DLLs, injection into svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe, and outbound to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "jshosting.me" or RemoteUrl endswith ".jshosting.me"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has "jshosting.me"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exploited AnySign4PC.exe spawning child process or dropping DLL AIExploitation High
Hunts the post-exploitation moment where the buffer-overflow in AnySign4PC.exe (Hancom Secure e-signature client) forces the signed process to spawn a child or write a DLL to disk with no user interaction. A certificate-signing client legitimately never spawns interpreters/LOLBins or drops DLLs, so either behaviour from AnySign4PC.exe is anomalous. Rationale: AnySign4PC.exe is the exact exploited binary named by ENKI/KISA; a signing client spawning children or dropping DLLs is behaviourally impossible in benign use, matching Plainbit's 'generated an error and created a malicious DLL without a download prompt'. Cross-checked against: • https://www.enki.co.kr/en/media-center/blog/joint-cybersecurity-advisory-watering-hole-malware-analysis • https://www.file.net/process/anysign4pc.exe.html
ATT&CKT1203 T1055 T1574.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AnySign4PC auto-update spawning its own updater/installer (AnySignUpdate.exe)
  • Crash-handler WerFault.exe launched by AnySign4PC after a benign fault
  • Vendor troubleshooting tool bundled with AnySign4PC launching a helper
  • EDR/AV telemetry stub injected into AnySign4PC being recorded as a child
Suppression filter
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySignUpdate.exe","AnySignSetup.exe") and not (FileName =~ "WerFault.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-p")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child process command line and any dropped DLL path/hash; a LOLBin (rundll32/regsvr32) child or a DLL written to ProgramData/Temp is a strong true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture memory (backdoor decrypts stages in memory and may be disk-absent), and record AnySign4PC version. 3) Hunt: pivot to svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe injection, net.tmp/inet.tmp artifacts, service-registry blobs, and C2 to 176.65.128[.]26 on the same device.
let ProcSpawn = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where FileName !in~ ("AnySign4PC.exe","AnySignUpdate.exe","conhost.exe","WerFault.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="ChildProcess", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
let DllDrop = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "AnySign4PC.exe"
| where ActionType == "FileCreated" and FileName endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="DllDrop", InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256;
ProcSpawn | union DllDrop
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe"
| where NewProcessName !endswith "\\AnySign4PC.exe" and NewProcessName !endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

C2 / reverse-SSH-tunnel to 176.65.128[.]26 (Operation Double Barrel infra) AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any outbound connection to 176.65.128[.]26, the reverse-tunnelling address AhnLab confirms was reused across both the state-sponsored SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE chain and the Gunra ransomware chain. Any egress to this fixed IP from a corporate host is a high-confidence compromise indicator. Rationale: 176.65.128[.]26 is a fixed IOC that AhnLab confirms as the reverse-tunnelling address shared across both operations — a rare dual-corroborated hard indicator that warrants direct alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://www.rescana.com/post/lazarus-group-exploits-anysign4pc-zero-day-to-target-south-korean-financial-sector-via-drive-by-attacks
ATT&CKT1572 T1071 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel validation traffic or IOC scanner probing the IP from a security appliance
  • Firewall logging the connection as denied (check DeviceAction=blocked before escalating)
  • Shared hosting rebind — verify the IP is still attacker-controlled at alert time
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus.exe","nmap.exe") and DeviceName !has "scanner"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe/SyncHost.exe or an unsigned binary reaching this IP is an immediate true positive; note the port (SSH/reverse-tunnel often 22/443). 2) Contain: block the IP org-wide, isolate the host, and preserve volatile memory before the loader's self-protection wipes disk artifacts. 3) Hunt: enumerate all internal hosts that contacted the IP, and on each check for Mimikatz/NLBrute, RDP fan-out, and service-registry C2 blobs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "176.65.128.26"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ApplicationProtocol, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected Microsoft process (SyncHost.exe / svchost.exe) making unexpected outbound connection AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the SIGNBT/COPPERHEDGE post-injection C2 pattern where shellcode is injected into legitimate SyncHost.exe or svchost.exe which then beacons out. SyncHost.exe reaching the public internet is inherently anomalous, and svchost.exe egress to the known C2 is a direct hit — both are the article's named injection targets in the espionage and Gunra chains. Rationale: The article and corroborating AhnLab report name svchost.exe and SyncHost.exe as the specific injection targets; SyncHost.exe public egress is behaviourally rare, and svchost.exe to the named C2 IP scopes the noisy svchost case to a hard indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1055.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SyncHost.exe legitimately syncing UWP/Mail-Calendar app data to Microsoft cloud endpoints (filter *.microsoft.com)
  • svchost.exe Windows Update / telemetry to Microsoft IP ranges (excluded via 20.* and MS domains)
  • Third-party sync client mis-named synchost.exe
  • Proxy/NAT collapsing many hosts behind one svchost egress record
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".live.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".office.com"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the remote IP is non-Microsoft; a SyncHost.exe connection to an unfamiliar VPS or the C2 IP is a true positive — pull the parent and any CreateRemoteThread (Sysmon 8) targeting the process. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture memory before the in-memory PE is wiped. 3) Hunt: check the same host for AnySign4PC exploitation, encrypted service-registry C2 blobs, and reverse-tunnel egress to 176.65.128[.]26.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "SyncHost.exe" and RemoteIPType == "Public")
     or (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and RemoteIP == "176.65.128.26")
| where RemoteIP !startswith "20." and RemoteUrl !endswith ".microsoft.com" and RemoteUrl !endswith ".windowsupdate.com"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "176.65.128.26") or (tolower(tostring(split(SrcHostname,"\\")[-1])) == "synchost.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SIGNBT/Gunra payload staging via net.tmp and inet.tmp AIInstallation High
Hunts creation or execution of the payload files net.tmp and inet.tmp — filenames AhnLab confirms were reused across both the state-sponsored and Gunra chains, with net.tmp invoked with a GUID-format argument. Detects both the file drop and the rundll32/loader execution referencing these temp payloads. Rationale: net.tmp and inet.tmp are exact malware filenames AhnLab confirms across both operations, with net.tmp carrying a GUID-format argument; matching them in command lines and file drops is high-fidelity and rarely benign. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011 T1027.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate installer or app that happens to write a temp file literally named net.tmp/inet.tmp (rare; verify parent and path)
  • Network-config tooling logging to a *net.tmp scratch file
  • Backup/AV quarantine renaming a file to net.tmp coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","svchost.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the file hash and the full command line — a GUID argument passed to net.tmp via rundll32/a loader is a strong true positive; the loader may side-load a DLL. 2) Contain: isolate the host and image memory (files may be deleted post-load and restored only at clean shutdown with a different hash). 3) Hunt: correlate with AnySign4PC exploitation, service-registry C2 blobs, and 176.65.128[.]26 egress; the same filenames appearing elsewhere may indicate the Gunra pre-ransomware stage.
let Drops = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="FileCreate", FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
let Exec = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("net.tmp","inet.tmp")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="Exec", FileName, FolderPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256;
Drops | union Exec
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "net.tmp" or CommandLine has "inet.tmp"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

logsource:

detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'net.tmp'
      - 'inet.tmp'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:1 AND @CommandLine:(*net.tmp* OR *inet.tmp* OR *NET.TMP* OR *INET.TMP*)) OR (@EventID:11 AND @TargetFilename:(*\net.tmp OR *\inet.tmp OR *\NET.TMP OR *\INET.TMP)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(^|\\|\s)i?net\.tmp/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*net.tmp*" OR Processes.process="*inet.tmp*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*net.tmp*" OR Processes.process="*inet.tmp*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
COPPERHEDGE/SIGNBT C2 config in service-registry blobs + unusual service creation AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the article's named persistence/C2-storage pattern: backdoors that read command-and-control information from encrypted blobs stored under service-registry entries, paired with unusual service creation. Flags registry value writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services whose ImagePath points at ProgramData/Temp/AppData. Rationale: The article and AhnLab explicitly recommend hunting 'encrypted data stored under service-registry entries' and 'unusual service creation'; scoping registry writes to CurrentControlSet\Services by non-installer processes and services running from ProgramData/Temp targets that exact tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1112 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate driver/service installers writing binary config under Services keys via a non-standard installer
  • EDR/AV agents storing encrypted config blobs under their own service key
  • Backup or management agents installed from ProgramData with a service entry
  • GPO/SCCM software deployment creating services from staging paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "setup.exe" and RegistryKey !has "Sense" and RegistryKey !has "WinDefend"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process and the service ImagePath — a rundll32/unsigned binary writing a REG_BINARY blob under a Services key, or a service pointing at Temp/ProgramData, is a true positive. 2) Contain: isolate the host, export the registry blob for offline decryption, and disable the rogue service. 3) Hunt: extract C2 from the decrypted blob and sweep for egress to those IPs plus 176.65.128[.]26, and check for svchost/SyncHost injection on the same host.
let SvcRegBlob = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueType == "Binary"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","poqexec.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcRegBlob", RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let SvcInstall = DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Signal="SvcInstall", RegistryKey=FolderPath, RegistryValueName=FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
SvcRegBlob | union SvcInstall
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7045
| where ServiceFileName has_any (@"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Users\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceStartType, SubjectUserName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*\CurrentControlSet\Services\* OR *\currentcontrolset\services\*) -@Image:(*\services.exe OR *\svchost.exe OR *\msiexec.exe OR *\TrustedInstaller.exe)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate RegObjectName=/\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/(services|svchost|msiexec|trustedinstaller)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_path="*\\CurrentControlSet\\Services\\*" AND Registry.registry_value_type="REG_BINARY" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_path Registry.registry_value_name Registry.process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`
| where NOT process_name IN ("services.exe","svchost.exe","msiexec.exe","TrustedInstaller.exe","System")
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| sort - lastTime
Anti-forensic evidence destruction: SDelete / CCleaner + 4-char rename-then-delete AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's named anti-forensic routine: renaming malicious files to random four-character names before deletion, with additional wiping via SDelete and CCleaner observed by Plainbit. Detects SDelete/CCleaner execution and the rename-to-4-char-name-then-delete file sequence. Rationale: Plainbit specifically observed SDelete and CCleaner used for evidence destruction, and AhnLab documented the rename-to-random-4-char-name-before-delete routine; combining the named tools with the rename/delete file pattern targets this exact anti-forensic tradecraft. Cross-checked against: • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/94696/ • https://image.ahnlab.com/atip/content/file/20260730/%5BAhnLab%5DOperation%20Double%20Barrel(ENG)(2026.07.30).pdf
ATT&CKT1070.004 T1485 T1070.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin using SDelete legitimately to securely wipe free space or decommission a disk
  • IT running CCleaner as a sanctioned cleanup/maintenance tool
  • Software installers creating short temp filenames that get renamed/deleted normally
  • Backup software renaming files to short hashes during dedup
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccleaner.exe","CCUpdate.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Program Files") and AccountName !in~ ("itadmin","backupsvc")
Response runbook
1) Triage: check who/what launched the wiper — SDelete/CCleaner run by a non-admin user, a service account, or a process descended from AnySign4PC/svchost is a true positive; correlate rename-to-4-char events on the same host and time window. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately (evidence is being destroyed) and preserve any remaining volatile memory and MFT. 3) Hunt: pivot to the same host's exploitation, injection, and C2 indicators before artifacts are gone, and check for lateral movement (RDP, NLBrute) to other hosts.
let Wipers = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (ProcessCommandLine has "sdelete" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-p","-s","-nobanner"))
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="WiperExec", FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName;
let RenameWipe = DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileRenamed"
| where FileName matches regex @"^[A-Za-z0-9]{4}(\.[A-Za-z0-9]{1,4})?$"
| where PreviousFileName endswith ".dll" or PreviousFileName endswith ".tmp" or PreviousFileName endswith ".exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="RenameToRandom", FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName=PreviousFileName;
Wipers | union RenameWipe
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("sdelete.exe","sdelete64.exe","CCleaner.exe","CCleaner64.exe")
     or (CommandLine has "sdelete" and CommandLine has_any ("-p","-nobanner"))
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Anti-Forensic Wiper SDelete / CCleaner Execution (Operation Double Barrel)

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.
ATT&CKT1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("176.65.128.26") or RemoteUrl has_any ("jshosting.me")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
let BadIPs     = dynamic(["176.65.128.26"]);
let BadDomains = dynamic(["jshosting.me"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in (BadIPs)
   or Url has_any (BadDomains)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, NetworkProtocol
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web

| join type=inner src

         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
